title: Solving PDEs: classical solvers and PINNs
summary: Partial differential equations are solved on grids by finite differences or volumes, with stability limits on the time step. PINNs solve them without grids. Learn both, and when each wins.
outcomes: discretise the heat equation with finite differences
explain and check the stability condition r ≤ 0.5
set up a PINN for a PDE with boundary and initial conditions
compare classical solvers and PINNs fairly
narration_en: Many systems vary in space as well as time: temperature in a pavement, pollution along a street, traffic density along a road. They obey partial differential equations. The classical way to solve them is to cut space and time into a grid. For the heat equation, the rate of change at a point is proportional to how much its neighbours differ from it, so each step updates every grid point from its neighbours. This explicit finite-difference scheme is simple, but it has a stability limit: the number r, the diffusivity times the time step divided by the square of the grid spacing, must stay at or below one half. Cross it and small wiggles grow until the solution explodes. For traffic, conservation laws are solved with finite-volume schemes such as Godunov's. A PINN takes a different route: it needs no grid, only collocation points in space and time, plus boundary and initial conditions in the loss. For simple forward problems a classical solver is usually faster and more accurate, but PINNs handle odd geometries, missing information and inverse problems. In this module you will push a solver past its stability limit.
narration_ar: كثير من الأنظمة تتغير في المكان كما تتغير في الزمن: درجة الحرارة في رصف الطريق، والتلوث على امتداد شارع، وكثافة المرور على طول طريق. وهي تخضع لمعادلات تفاضلية جزئية. والطريقة الكلاسيكية لحلها هي تقطيع المكان والزمان إلى شبكة. ففي معادلة الحرارة يتناسب معدل التغير عند نقطة مع مقدار اختلاف جيرانها عنها، فتُحدَّث كل نقطة في الشبكة في كل خطوة انطلاقاً من جيرانها. هذا المخطط الصريح للفروق المحدودة بسيط، لكن له حد استقرار: العدد r، وهو معامل الانتشار مضروباً في الخطوة الزمنية مقسوماً على مربع تباعد الشبكة، يجب أن يبقى عند النصف أو دونه. فإذا تجاوزه نمت التموجات الصغيرة حتى ينفجر الحل. وفي المرور تُحل قوانين الحفظ بمخططات الحجوم المحدودة مثل مخطط غودونوف. أما الشبكة المستنيرة بالفيزياء فتسلك طريقاً آخر: لا تحتاج إلى شبكة، بل إلى نقاط تجميع في المكان والزمان، إضافة إلى الشروط الحدية والابتدائية في دالة الخسارة. وفي المسائل الأمامية البسيطة يكون الحل الكلاسيكي عادة أسرع وأدق، لكن الشبكات المستنيرة تتعامل مع الأشكال الهندسية الغريبة والمعلومات الناقصة والمسائل العكسية. ستدفع في هذه الوحدة مُحلاً إلى ما بعد حد استقراره.

diagram.title: Two ways to solve a PDE
diagram.caption: A grid-based solver marches in time under a stability limit; a PINN minimises residuals at scattered points.

nodes.label: PDE + conditions
nodes.detail: The equation plus boundary conditions (ends held at zero) and an initial condition (starting temperature profile).

nodes.label: Grid
nodes.detail: Space cut into points Δx apart; time into steps Δt.

nodes.label: Finite differences
nodes.detail: u_i ← u_i + r (u_{i+1} − 2u_i + u_{i−1}), r = αΔt/Δx².

nodes.label: Stability
nodes.detail: Explicit schemes blow up if r > 0.5. Implicit schemes are stable but need a linear solve each step.

nodes.label: PINN
nodes.detail: Network u(x, t); loss = residual at random (x, t) + boundary + initial terms.

nodes.label: Compare
nodes.detail: Classical: fast, accurate for forward problems. PINN: flexible geometry, data fusion, inverse problems.

tour.text: Start from the equation and its boundary and initial conditions.
The classical route: a grid, and updates from neighbours.
Explicit updates are stable only if r ≤ 0.5.
The PINN route: no grid, a residual loss at scattered points.

sections.heading: Finite differences for heat
sections.html:
Approximate the second derivative by neighbours: ∂²u/∂x² ≈ (ui+1 − 2ui + ui−1)/Δx². With an Euler step in time:

uin+1 = uin + r (ui+1n − 2uin + ui−1n), r = αΔt/Δx²

A hot point loses heat to cooler neighbours; a cold point gains. Ends are held at zero (boundary conditions).

sections.heading: Stability: the r ≤ 0.5 rule
sections.html: The explicit scheme is stable only for r ≤ 0.5 (von Neumann analysis). In the lab with 41 points: r = 0.25 and r = 0.5 give errors below 0.0004, r = 0.52 gives 0.12, and r = 0.6 explodes to 107. Halving Δx forces a quarter of the time step, which is why implicit schemes (Crank–Nicolson) are used for fine grids.

sections.heading: Traffic: finite volumes
sections.html: Conservation laws such as the LWR traffic model have shock waves (sudden jams), where finite differences oscillate. Finite-volume schemes track how many vehicles cross each cell boundary; Godunov's scheme (in traffic, the cell transmission model of Daganzo 1994) takes the smaller of upstream demand and downstream supply. Module 3.1 uses it as the physics inside a traffic state estimator. Its time step obeys the CFL condition: vfΔt/Δx ≤ 1.

sections.heading: A PINN for the heat equation
sections.html: Network u(x, t); loss = mean (ut − uxx)² at 1,000 random points, plus boundary terms u(0,t)² + u(1,t)², plus initial term (u(x,0) − sin πx)². The PyTorch lab trains in about 20 seconds and reaches a maximum error of about 0.04 at t = 0.1, while the finite-difference solver gets below 0.001 in a fraction of a second. For this forward problem the classical solver wins; PINNs earn their place when data must be fused or parameters inferred.

callouts.title: Try it
callouts.html: Set r = 0.49, then 0.51. Look closely at the profile: where do the first wiggles appear?

callouts.title: Fair comparison
callouts.html: Papers sometimes compare a carefully tuned PINN with a crude classical solver. Compare at equal accuracy or equal computing time.

takeaways: Grid solvers update each point from its neighbours.
Explicit finite differences for heat need r = αΔt/Δx² ≤ 0.5.
Finite-volume (Godunov) schemes handle traffic shock waves under a CFL limit.
PINNs need no grid; classical solvers usually win simple forward problems.

glossary.def: Approximating derivatives by differences between neighbouring grid values.
Tracking conserved quantities by fluxes across cell boundaries.
A limit on step sizes beyond which numerical errors grow without bound.
Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy limit: information must not travel more than one cell per step.
